title: The Fed holds, but leans toward hiking
deck: The Federal Reserve left rates at 3.75-4% on 28 October with two voters demanding a hike, and Treasury Secretary Bessent said another hike would not necessarily be a mistake, which keeps the dollar firm and tightens the squeeze on Japan, Europe and Canada.

fuel.title: US inflation concerns weigh on Fed
fuel.how: Price pressure that keeps rising, as reported on the day, leaves the Fed no room to ease and two voters wanting to hike.

fuel.title: Bessent open to another Fed hike
fuel.how: The Treasury Secretary said a further hike would 'not necessarily' be a mistake, signalling government tolerance for tighter policy.

fuel.title: Firm dollar presses yen near 158
fuel.how: A hawkish Fed keeps US yields high and the dollar firm, which pressures the yen before the Bank of Japan decides on 30 October.

fuel.title: Gulf war keeps oil costs elevated
fuel.how: Strikes on Iran since 28 February 2026 have kept oil and freight costs high for eight months, feeding the price pressure the Fed is fighting.

card.headline: The Fed held rates, but half a step from hiking

keyNumber.label: Fed voters dissented on 28 October, both wanting a quarter-point hike; the range stayed at 3.75-4%

forYou.line: Rates stay at 3.75-4% and the talk is of hikes, not cuts. Do not plan around cheaper credit soon.
A firm dollar and high US yields are the main channel to other markets. Watch the ECB on 29 October and the Bank of Japan on 30 October.
USD/JPY is near 158. A strong dollar helps US-based sellers abroad less than it hurts those who buy in dollars.
Part of the inflation behind this is oil. While the Gulf war continues, the Fed has less room to ease.

effects.text: The Fed left its target range at 3.75-4% despite inflation that is reported to be rising
Two of 12 voters dissented, both wanting a quarter-point rise, which shows the committee's tilt
Treasury Secretary Bessent said it would 'not necessarily' be a mistake if the Fed hiked again
Gulf-war oil and freight costs, elevated for eight months, remain part of the price pressure
US yields stay high and the dollar firm; USD/JPY sits near 158
The ECB meets on 29 October with euro-area inflation at 3.8% and French bond stress in the background
US borrowing costs stay high for households and firms, with no easing in sight
Treasury tolerance for tightening lowers the political cost of a hawkish Fed
The Bank of Japan, at 1.25% and meeting on 30 October, faces pressure to signal 1.5% as early as December
A hawkish Fed weighs on other economies, including Japan, Germany and Canada, through capital flows

whatHappened: On 28 October 2026 the US Federal Reserve left its interest rate target unchanged at 3.75-4%. It did so even as inflation, in the words of one report, continues to rise.
The decision was not unanimous. Two of the 12 voting members of the Federal Open Market Committee dissented. Both wanted to raise rates by a quarter of a percentage point.
The same day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC it would 'not necessarily' be a mistake if the Fed raised rates again. That is unusual support for tighter policy from the government side.
whyItMatters: Living costs: the Fed is holding because inflation will not fade. The reports we have say it is still rising, though they do not give the level. Two of 12 voters wanted to hike. So the question for borrowers is no longer when rates fall, but whether they rise.

Politics: Bessent's comment tells markets the Treasury will not push back against a hike. That makes a further rise easier to deliver and raises the chance that the Fed's next move is up rather than down.

Markets: a Fed that leans hawkish keeps US yields high and the dollar firm. That moves capital worldwide. USD/JPY is near 158, which pressures the yen ahead of the Bank of Japan's 30 October meeting. The ECB meets on 29 October, a day after the Fed, with its own inflation problem.

Energy: strikes on Iran that began on 28 February 2026 have kept oil and freight costs elevated for eight months. Higher energy costs feed into prices, which is part of why the Fed cannot ease. French diesel hit a record EUR 2.41 a litre in September.

winners.who: Holders of dollars and dollar assets
winners.why: High US rates and a firm dollar favour them, at least while the Fed leans hawkish.
With rates at 3.75-4% and no cuts in sight, returns on cash and short-term deposits stay relatively high. This is our inference, not a figure from the sources.
Two voters pushed for a hike and the Treasury Secretary has now said a hike would not necessarily be wrong.

losers.why: Mortgages, car loans and business credit stay expensive while rates are held high with a hike on the table.
A firm dollar pushes USD/JPY near 158, which raises the cost of dollar-priced imports such as oil.

losers.who: Economies such as Germany and Canada
losers.why: The summary notes a hawkish Fed tilt weighs on them through the dollar and capital flows.
The ECB and Bank of Japan must decide with US rates high and their currencies under pressure.

whatsNext: 29 October: the ECB meets after euro-area inflation rose to 3.8% in September.
30 October: the Bank of Japan concludes its meeting with its rate at 1.25%, and publishes its Quarterly Outlook Report.
9 December: the next scheduled Fed meeting (date from the published calendar; worth confirming). A second round of dissent, or a hike, is the thing to watch.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely Fed move at its next meeting in December?
predict.explanation: Our base case is another hold, at about 60%. Two of 12 voters already want a hike, so a hike is the main alternative. A cut looks unlikely while inflation is reported to be rising.

timeline.title: Strikes on Iran begin
timeline.detail: The US-Israel campaign starts an energy shock. Oil and freight costs stay elevated for eight months, worsened later by fighting in Yemen and attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure.

timeline.title: French diesel hits a record EUR 2.41 a litre
timeline.detail: A visible sign of the energy shock feeding into consumer prices in Europe. Month given only; exact day not in our material.

timeline.title: Euro-area inflation rises to 3.8%
timeline.detail: September reading. ECB minutes show policymakers weighing another rate rise, with French bond stress adding pressure.

timeline.title: Bank of Japan hikes to 1.25%
timeline.detail: A 7-2 vote lifts the rate to its highest since April 1995. It is the shortest gap between hikes since 1990.

timeline.title: Fed holds at 3.75-4%
timeline.detail: Rates are unchanged despite inflation that is reported to be rising. Two of 12 voters dissent, both wanting a quarter-point hike.

timeline.title: Bessent says a hike would not necessarily be a mistake
timeline.detail: Speaking to CNBC the same day, the Treasury Secretary signals tolerance for tighter policy.

timeline.title: ECB meeting (scheduled)
timeline.detail: The first major central bank decision after the Fed hold. The Bank of France governor says France's bond problem must be solved at home.

timeline.title: Bank of Japan decision and Outlook Report (scheduled)
timeline.detail: Markets expect a hold but watch for guidance toward 1.5% as early as December. USD/JPY trades near 158.

timeline.title: Next Fed meeting (scheduled)
timeline.detail: The first test of whether the two hike dissents become a majority. Date is from the published calendar and is not in our sources.

causes.name: Inflation that has been hard to shake
causes.detail: The sources describe inflation as continuing to rise. That limits any move toward easing, though we do not have the level.

causes.name: Dollar at the centre of global finance
causes.detail: US policy moves capital, currencies and borrowing costs well beyond America, which is why the Fed's tone matters to Japan, Germany and Canada.

causes.name: A hold with a hawkish tilt
causes.detail: The committee left rates unchanged but two of 12 voters dissented in favour of a quarter-point hike.

causes.name: Treasury support for tightening
causes.detail: Bessent said another hike would 'not necessarily' be a mistake, removing a possible political brake.

causes.name: Gulf war energy shock
causes.detail: Oil and freight costs have been elevated for eight months since strikes on Iran began on 28 February.

causes.name: Parallel inflation elsewhere
causes.detail: Euro-area inflation at 3.8% and Japan's flagged oil risk mean other central banks are also leaning toward tightening, so the dollar is not the only story.

stakeholders.name: The Federal Open Market Committee majority
stakeholders.wants: Time to judge whether inflation is turning, without overtightening
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold again unless the data worsen, while keeping a hike on the table

stakeholders.name: The two dissenting voters
stakeholders.wants: Tighter policy now to stop inflation spreading
stakeholders.leverage: Their dissents shift the committee's tone and the market's expectations
stakeholders.likelyMove: Dissent again in December if inflation does not ease

stakeholders.name: Scott Bessent
stakeholders.wants: Not stated beyond his comment; he signalled he would not oppose a hike
stakeholders.leverage: A voice in government and with markets
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep describing a further hike as an option, not a mistake

stakeholders.name: Bank of Japan (Governor Ueda)
stakeholders.wants: Steady normalisation as underlying inflation nears 2%
stakeholders.leverage: Decides whether to signal a move toward 1.5% as early as December
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold on 30 October, with hawkish guidance

stakeholders.name: European Central Bank
stakeholders.wants: Contain 3.8% inflation without worsening French bond stress
stakeholders.likelyMove: Decide on its own inflation, not the Fed's; the two banks are answering separate problems

stakeholders.name: US households and businesses
stakeholders.wants: Lower borrowing costs and stable prices
stakeholders.leverage: Spending and political pressure, as midterm elections arrive on 3 November
stakeholders.likelyMove: Delay big purchases and borrowing while rate cuts look distant

stakeholders.name: Gulf war parties and oil producers
stakeholders.wants: Their own military and political aims
stakeholders.leverage: Control of oil supply and shipping routes
stakeholders.likelyMove: Any escalation raises oil, and therefore inflation, and so the case for tighter policy

sectors.why: Rates held at 3.75-4% with hikes on the table keep mortgages and loans costly.
A hawkish Fed keeps US yields high and the dollar firm; USD/JPY is near 158.
A weak yen raises import costs, notably for oil priced in dollars, even as it helps exporters.
High policy rates support yields, but the market will also weigh how far the Fed may go and the effect on growth.
The Gulf shock keeps prices high, but a strong dollar and tight policy can restrain demand.
A firm dollar and high global rates add to their borrowing and import-cost pressure.
Higher-for-longer rates can lift deposit and lending margins but also strain borrowers. This is an inference, not a sourced figure.

dailyLife.effect: With the Fed on hold at 3.75-4% and hikes discussed, expect no near-term relief on borrowing costs.
The Fed is holding because inflation is reported to be rising. Energy costs are a piece of that, given eight months of an elevated oil and freight bill.
French diesel hit a record EUR 2.41 a litre in September. US pump prices are not in our material, but the same oil market applies.
Cash yields should stay relatively high while rates stay put. We have not seen specific bank rates.
A firm dollar against a yen near 158 makes yen-priced goods and travel cheaper for dollar holders. This is our inference.

scenarios.name: Extended hold
scenarios.looksLike: The Fed holds at 3.75-4% through the winter. The two hawks stay in the minority and inflation stays high but does not worsen sharply.
signposts: No further rise in inflation readings
scenarios.effectOnWorld: The dollar stays firm but stable. The Bank of Japan and ECB make their own calls, and pressure on the yen persists without a crisis.

scenarios.name: Fed hikes
scenarios.looksLike: Inflation keeps rising, a majority joins the two dissenters, and the Fed raises by a quarter point in December or early 2027.
signposts: Worse inflation data or an oil spike
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Stronger dollar, more strain on the yen, euro and Canadian dollar, and tighter global financial conditions.

scenarios.name: Inflation cools, easing returns
scenarios.looksLike: Oil eases and inflation stops rising. The Fed holds for a while and the talk shifts back to cuts in 2027.
signposts: A de-escalation of the Gulf war
scenarios.effectOnWorld: The dollar softens and the yen recovers, giving the Bank of Japan more room.

scenarios.name: Disorderly market reaction
scenarios.looksLike: A hawkish surprise or an energy shock triggers sharp moves in currencies and bond markets, forcing emergency policy responses.
signposts: Sudden jumps in US or French bond yields
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Global risk-off, with pressure on weaker currencies and heavily indebted governments.

predictions.text: The Fed will hold rates at 3.75-4% at its December meeting (probability 0.6).
At least one FOMC voter will again dissent in favour of a hike at the December meeting (probability 0.6).
The Bank of Japan will leave its rate at 1.25% on 30 October (probability 0.8; markets expect a hold).
USD/JPY will still be above 150 at the end of 2026 (probability 0.75).
The Fed will raise its target range at least once by mid-2027 (probability 0.35).

actions: Assume borrowing costs stay at today's level or higher through 2027 and stress-test plans for a hike.
Hedge dollar exposure, especially for yen, euro and Canadian dollar flows.
Build fuel and freight surcharges into contracts while the Gulf war keeps energy costs elevated.
Watch the ECB on 29 October and the Bank of Japan on 30 October, since both react to a firm dollar.
Treat the dissents and Bessent's comment as a signal that hikes are live, not a base case.
Note that the sources do not give exact market moves; check live yields and USD/JPY before acting.
Do not wait for rate cuts before deciding on a major loan; fix a rate if you need certainty.
Keep an emergency buffer, since higher prices and rates both squeeze budgets.
Compare savings accounts, as cash yields should stay relatively high.
Communicate clearly on whether a further hike is a real option, since mixed signals from the Fed and Treasury move markets.
Coordinate with other central banks on dollar pressure, notably on the yen.
Address the energy shock directly, since it is part of the inflation that limits monetary easing.

analogues.whatFollowed: Fed rates rose from near zero to above 5% in about 16 months. The dollar strengthened sharply, pressured the yen and other currencies, and Japan intervened in currency markets in autumn 2022.

analogues.event: Fed doubles rates and bond rout
analogues.whatFollowed: A sharp, surprising tightening hit bond markets worldwide and was followed by Mexico's peso crisis in December 1994.
Hints of Fed tightening drove capital out of emerging markets and weakened several currencies, showing how a Fed signal moves other economies.

evidence.method: Drafted from the three listed sources, three matched wire headlines and the summaries of three connected events. We had headlines and short summaries only, not full articles or market data, so figures such as the inflation level, yields and exchange rates were not available and are not given. The scheduled dates for the December Fed meeting and the US midterms come from general knowledge, and all scenario probabilities and predictions are estimates.
